questions.q: In one line, what is a parabolic long?
choices: The turn after a 3 to 5 day drop
Riding a stock up its run
A breakout from a quiet base
A bottom built over months
questions.answer: The turn after a 3 to 5 day drop
questions.why: The turn after a 3 to 5 day panic drop. We trade Bracco's parabolic burst turned upside down: a stock falls straight down for days, then snaps back. We buy only after the turn, never during the fall. It is the opposite of riding a stock up its run.
questions.lesson_line: A parabolic long buys the snap back, not the fall.

wrong.Riding a stock up its run: That is buying the run up, the opposite trade. Ours is the mirror of a burst down.
wrong.A breakout from a quiet base: A quiet base is a rest. This setup has no rest; it is a panic fall and a turn.
wrong.A bottom built over months: The card describes a straight-down fall of 3 to 5 days, not a slow bottom.

questions.simple: A parabolic long buys the snap back after a fast 3 to 5 day panic drop, not the drop itself.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26: the long is the mirror of Bracco's burst down)
fixed before: touched by the old Model Book card question (D-014)

questions.q: Our parabolic long is Bracco's parabolic burst mirrored: three straight down days, two gap downs, rising volume.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our rulebook makes the parabolic long the mirror image of Bracco's burst, a burst down. Bracco's own post has no parabolic long. The card lists three straight lower closes, two gap-down opens, bigger losses, rising volume and a climax gap down.
questions.lesson_line: Read Bracco's burst upside down. That is our parabolic long.
questions.simple: True. We read Bracco's burst upside down, so the long is three down days, two gap downs and rising volume.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, confirmed 'yes')

questions.q: What is the target of a parabolic long?
choices: The daily 9 EMA, from below
The 50-day average, from below
The high before the fall began
A set percent bounce off the low
questions.answer: The daily 9 EMA, from below
questions.why: The daily 9 EMA, from below. Bracco uses it as the target for his parabolic short, and our card keeps it for the long. The trade is done when price gets there.
questions.lesson_line: The 9 EMA is the finish line. The trade is done when price gets there.

wrong.The 50-day average, from below: The card names the daily 9 EMA as the target, not the 50-day.
wrong.The high before the fall began: The card's target is the 9 EMA. The old high is not in the plan.
wrong.A set percent bounce off the low: The card targets an average, not a percent. The 9 EMA moves with the stock.

questions.simple: The target is the daily 9 EMA, from below. It is Bracco's short target, kept in our card for the long.

deeper.counter: Bracco calls the 9 EMA a magnet for his short. Our card keeps it for the long as the finish line: the trade is done when price gets there.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D47) and on the card's own test of longs (c19)
the exit is part of the held trim question (D-013)

questions.q: Our 200-day rule bars stocks below the line. What may we buy under it?
choices: Index or 2x-3x ETF, parabolic long
A stock, on a parabolic long setup
A stock that is down 30% from its high
A stock pulling back to its 50-day line
questions.answer: Index or 2x-3x ETF, parabolic long
questions.why: An index or a 2x-3x ETF on a parabolic long. Below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks. The one exception is an index or an ETF built to move two or three times the index, bought on a parabolic long. A parabolic long also needs no RS rating.
questions.lesson_line: Below the 200-day, stocks are a no. An index or 2x-3x ETF on a parabolic long is the exception.

wrong.A stock, on a parabolic long setup: Below the 200-day, stocks are a hard no, even in a parabolic burst. Only an index or a 2x-3x ETF gets the exception.
wrong.A stock that is down 30% from its high: A percent fall is not the exception. Below the 200-day, a stock is a hard no.
wrong.A stock pulling back to its 50-day line: A pullback is a normal long. Below the 200-day, a stock is a hard no.

questions.simple: Stocks are a hard no below the 200-day line. Only an index or a 2x-3x ETF may be bought there, on a parabolic long.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
its narrowing is a held decision (D-009)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Our buy day is the ___ day, the gap-down day.
questions.answer: climax
questions.why: The climax day. The buy day is the climax day, the gap-down day. Even then you buy only after the turn, on the first 5-minute close back over VWAP.
questions.lesson_line: The buy day is the climax day. Not the day before, and not a week later.
questions.simple: The buy day is the climax day, the gap-down day. You still wait for the turn before you buy.

reasons: stable definition from the criteria card; no number that changes

questions.q: A parabolic long needs an RS rating of 80 or more, like the other longs we buy.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The rule to buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in one of the strongest groups, exempts parabolic and mean-reversion trades. The card says the same: no RS requirement for parabolic trades.
questions.lesson_line: RS does not apply here. Parabolic trades are exempt from the leader rule.
questions.simple: False. Our RS 80 rule is for leaders, and parabolic trades are exempt from it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)

questions.q: The trigger prints. Bracco's short takes a second entry later. How does our long enter?
choices: One market buy, full size at once
A second buy over the day's high
A limit order well under the reclaim
Half now, half later at the 9 EMA
questions.answer: One market buy, full size at once
questions.why: One market buy, full size. The card says a market order when the trigger prints, the full size at one price, no second entry. Our rulebook says the same: entries are market orders, no adding. Bracco's short takes a second entry when it breaks below the day's lows; the long gets no mirror of that.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, one trade. The second entry is not ours.

wrong.A second buy over the day's high: That mirrors Bracco's second entry on the short. Our long has no second entry.
wrong.A limit order well under the reclaim: Our entries are market orders when the trigger prints.
wrong.Half now, half later at the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA is where the trade ends, not where it grows.

questions.simple: We buy the full size once, at market, at one price. Bracco's second entry is not in our rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)
rebalanced choices: the old key was the longest

questions.q: On the climax day, when exactly is the buy?
choices: First 5-minute close over VWAP
The first print after the gap-down
The day's last print, at the close
A buy stop over the prior high
questions.answer: First 5-minute close over VWAP
questions.why: The first 5-minute close back above VWAP, after the low is in. Never before the turn. Bracco's short waits for a break under VWAP; our long waits for the reclaim. The order is a market order when the trigger prints.
questions.lesson_line: The right side of the V. VWAP reclaimed, after the low, is the buy.

wrong.A buy stop over the prior high: The card buys the VWAP reclaim at market, not with a stop order over a prior high.
wrong.The first print after the gap-down: That is buying the knife, the gap or the low before the turn. The card says never before the turn.
wrong.The day's last print, at the close: The buy is the intraday reclaim, the first 5-minute bar that closes back over VWAP, not the close.

questions.simple: Buy the first 5-minute close back above VWAP, after the low is in, and never before the turn.

deeper.trap: The named mistake is buying the knife: buying the gap or the low before the intraday turn. Bracco warns that shorting at the day's highs can be a dangerous trap, and the long mirrors it. A gap-down open that has not yet reclaimed VWAP is still falling.

reasons: the trigger is the card's default while D-003 is pending
mirrors Bracco's VWAP rule (p10)

questions.q: On the climax-day entry the stop sits a few cents under the climax day's low.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it. Bracco exits his short if the day's high is reclaimed; the mirror for our long is the day's low. Stop first: the size then comes from the distance to it.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the climax low.
questions.simple: True. The stop goes a few cents under the climax day's low, not right on it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: By Bracco's post mirrored, how long is the burst down?
choices: 3 to 5 sessions
One day
Two to three weeks
A month or more
questions.answer: 3 to 5 sessions
questions.why: 3 to 5 sessions. Bracco calls the burst a 3-5 day move that marks the final leg. The climax gap usually comes on day 3 to 5. The long reads it mirrored, as a drop. A longer fall is a decline or a grind, not the burst.
questions.lesson_line: Three to five days of panic, then the climax. Longer is a decline, not a burst.

wrong.One day: A one-day flush in a leader is Mean Reversion, not this card. The burst needs 3 to 5 sessions.
wrong.Two to three weeks: Weeks is a decline, not the burst. The burst is the 3 to 5 day accelerating end of a fall.
wrong.A month or more: A slow grind lower is not this setup. The burst is an accelerating 3 to 5 sessions.

questions.simple: The burst is the last fast leg of the fall, and it lasts 3 to 5 days. Longer than that is just a decline.

reasons: Bracco's burst length and the card agree; two facts

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The smallest climax-day volume we accept is ___ times its 50-day average.
questions.why: 2 times. Our climax day ends at 2 times its 50-day average volume or more, with volume rising through the burst. Bracco's fourth box is two days of rising volume.
questions.lesson_line: A climax without a crowd is not a climax. Two times average, rising.
questions.simple: A climax needs a crowd, so the day's volume must reach at least 2 times the 50-day average.

reasons: +3 the 2x line rests on one cited fact (c06)
+2 a threshold that is a card proposal and can change

questions.q: A close under the lower Bollinger band the day before is the trigger to buy.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A close under the lower band the day before is a plus, not a trigger. Bracco says a band breach is usually short-lived and often precedes a snap back. We read one as stretched, not a bottom call. The trigger is the first 5-minute close back over VWAP on the climax day.
questions.lesson_line: Outside the Bollinger band says stretched. It does not say buy.
questions.simple: False, because closing under the lower band only says the stock is stretched. The buy comes later, at the VWAP reclaim.

reasons: stable; Bracco and the card agree

questions.q: Which decline is parabolic?
choices: Steeper legs, little overlap
A stair-step, dips bought
A drift under the 50-day
A fall that slows each leg
questions.answer: Steeper legs, little overlap
questions.why: Steeper legs, little bar overlap. The fall accelerates, and an orderly, overlapping decline is not this setup. Bulkowski's vertical run down has the same feature: minimal overlap from bar to bar.
questions.lesson_line: Parabolic means accelerating. A stair-step is a different animal.

wrong.A stair-step, dips bought: A stair-step is orderly and overlapping. The setup needs a fall that accelerates.
wrong.A drift under the 50-day: A slow grind lower is the worst setting for this setup, and it has no climax.
wrong.A fall that slows each leg: Slowing legs are the opposite of the test. The setup needs each leg steeper.

questions.simple: A parabolic fall gets steeper each leg and the bars hardly overlap. A slow or orderly decline is a different thing.

reasons: one choice replaced to remove a silly option; Bulkowski site blocks plain downloads

questions.q: Parabolic long candidate?
questions.story: A stock off a recent high broke a three-month support level yesterday for the first time. Today is its second straight down day. It closes near its low on heavy volume.
choices: No; only day two of a breakdown
Yes; heavy volume means capitulation
Yes, if it reclaims VWAP tomorrow
No; it is not under its 200-day yet
questions.answer: No; only day two of a breakdown
questions.why: No. The first or second day of a breakdown from a top is not this setup. Bracco passed on a long on a second down day that was also the first break of a 3-month support level. A burst needs 3 to 5 days.
questions.lesson_line: Day two of a breakdown is the start of the fall, not the end.

wrong.Yes; heavy volume means capitulation: Heavy volume on day two is the selling starting, not finishing.
wrong.Yes, if it reclaims VWAP tomorrow: A reclaim needs a burst behind it. Two days is not a burst.
wrong.No; it is not under its 200-day yet: The 200-day is not a condition. A parabolic long may sit under it, but it does not have to.

questions.simple: No, because it is only day two of a breakdown. The fall has barely started, so there is no panic to buy yet.

reasons: card line plus Bracco's pass; the pass was on QQQ, an index, so the wording stays general

questions.q: We make no new buys in the 3 days before a company's earnings report.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. Our GE example shows the risk: its trade was still open when the 04-22 report gapped it up, so the hold carried earnings risk.
questions.lesson_line: The calendar comes before the chart. In the 3 days before a report, no new buy.
questions.simple: True. We do not open a new buy in the 3 days before an earnings report.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)
the question says 3 sessions, the rulebook says 3 days

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five mirrored boxes?
choices: Volume at 2x the 50-day average
Three straight days of lower closes
Two straight overnight gap downs
Two days of rising volume
questions.answer: Volume at 2x the 50-day average
questions.why: Volume at 2 times the 50-day average is not a box. It is a separate test: the climax day ends at 2 times its 50-day average volume or more. The five boxes: three straight lower closes, two gap-down opens, two of the three days losing more than the day before, two days of rising volume, and a gap down on the climax day.
questions.lesson_line: Count the five boxes. The 2x volume test is separate, not a box.

wrong.Three straight days of lower closes: Box one. Bracco's three straight days of gains, mirrored.
wrong.Two straight overnight gap downs: Box two. The climax day may be the second gap.
wrong.Two days of rising volume: Box four. Each day's volume is higher than the last.

questions.simple: The 2x volume test is a separate test, not one of the five boxes.

reasons: the box count is a held decision (D-002)

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: You bought the VWAP reclaim at 41.20 with the stop a few cents under the day's low. At 1:30 it loses VWAP, the day's low breaks and the price trades through your stop.
choices: Out; the stop has done its job
Hold; give it room until the close
Add; it is cheaper than the fill
Move the stop under the week's low
questions.answer: Out; the stop has done its job
questions.why: Out. The entry bar failed back under VWAP, the day's low broke and the price went through the stop. The stop is the exit and it only moves up, never down or wider. A new low means the selling was not done.
questions.lesson_line: Lose VWAP and the low, and the thesis is wrong. The stop says so first.

wrong.Hold; give it room until the close: A stop does not wait for the close. It is the exit.
wrong.Add; it is cheaper than the fill: Never add when down. The rule is the full size at one price.
wrong.Move the stop under the week's low: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.simple: Get out. Price lost VWAP and broke the day's low, so the stop is the exit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)
fixed before: the story said only 'a new low', which may not reach a stop a few cents under the old low

questions.q: The trigger prints at 20.00. Three minutes later it trades 21.00. Buy?
choices: No; 5% over is past our limit
Yes; 5% over is momentum
Yes, but only at half size
No; a buy over 20.00 chases
questions.answer: No; 5% over is past our limit
questions.why: No. 21.00 is 5% over the 20.00 trigger and our line is 4%, so we skip it. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays put, the distance to it grows, and the shares shrink. A buy up to 4% over the trigger is still inside the rule.
questions.lesson_line: A snap back moves fast. Past 4% over the trigger, let it go.

wrong.Yes; 5% over is momentum: Confirmed and too far away are both true. The chase line is 4%.
wrong.Yes, but only at half size: Half of a chased entry is still chased. The rule is to skip it, not to shrink it.
wrong.No; a buy over 20.00 chases: Chasing starts past 4% over the buy point. A small step above the trigger is allowed.

questions.simple: No. The price is 5% over the trigger, and our rule skips anything more than 4% over.

deeper.example: The stop is the day's low and it does not move. At 20.00 the distance to the stop is already set. At 21.00 that distance is larger, so the same risk buys fewer shares, and the trade has less room before the target. The chase line stops that drift at 4%.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
computed key (5% from the calc)

questions.q: The 50-day is 180.00, ATR 4.00, the close before the climax day 150.00. How many ATR under the 50-day is it?
questions.answer: 7.5 ATR
questions.why: 7.5 ATR. Take the 50-day minus the close, then divide by the ATR: (180.00 minus 150.00) divided by 4.00 is 7.5. Our card lists this stretch for each example, such as BABA at 6.7 ATR under its 50-day. It shows how far price ran in terms of its own normal range.
questions.lesson_line: Stretch is measured in ATRs under the 50-day. Do the division.
questions.simple: Subtract the close from the 50-day, then divide by the ATR, and you get 7.5 ATR.

reasons: computed key
the ATR cut-offs are a held decision (D-118); this item only computes the stretch

choices: 30.0 ATR
0.1 ATR
7.5 ATR

wrong.30.0 ATR: Gave the gap in dollars, no divide.
wrong.120.0 ATR: Multiplied by the ATR instead of dividing.
wrong.0.1 ATR: Flipped it: divided the ATR by the gap.

questions.q: The stop on a parabolic long can wait in your head, since the trade lasts just days.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head, however short the trade. Kullamagi calls the parabolic setups by far the riskiest if you do not obey your stops. A gap can still jump a stop; for that we have the gap rule.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. Put it with the broker.
questions.simple: False. Every position needs a real stop order with the broker, even a short trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41)

questions.q: Which backdrop makes the parabolic long strongest?
choices: When the index capitulates too
In a calm market, drifting up
On day one of a market breakdown
When one stock falls on its own
questions.answer: When the index capitulates too
questions.why: When the index is capitulating too. The best case: an index at least 3 ATR under its 50-day, a gap down of 1 ATR or more, a Monday. A fast VIX move into 30 and deeply oversold breadth add to it. A crowded group unwinding at once is the other top setting. Kell says the same: get aggressive when the index prints the reversal.
questions.lesson_line: One stock crashing is a story. The whole market crashing is a setup.

wrong.In a calm market, drifting up: A calm index weakens the case. There is no market panic to snap back from.
wrong.On day one of a market breakdown: Day one is the start of the fall. The burst comes later.
wrong.When one stock falls on its own: A lone stock is a weaker case than a market-wide panic. A crowded group or the index unwinding is the best setting.

questions.simple: The long works best when the whole market is panicking too, not when only one stock is falling.

deeper.example: DB on Monday 2024-08-05, the day of the yen carry unwind. It fell 19.7% in 9 sessions and printed four boxes. It gapped down 4.2% on 2.3x volume. Buy 14.08, stop 13.67, and 3R came in 9 sessions.

reasons: card line plus Kell and Bracco; proposed card context

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The trade is done when price reaches the daily ___ EMA from below.
questions.why: The 9 EMA. Bracco's studies make the 9 EMA the magnet; our rulebook keeps it as the parabolic target.
questions.lesson_line: Nine. The daily 9 EMA from below is where this trade ends.

questions.q: Buy the close, or wait?
questions.story: It is Friday. The index is four down days deep and stretched under its 50-day. The VIX is 28. A liquid ETF has three boxes and a green close.
choices: Wait; Monday may bring a flush
Buy the close; the turn is in
Buy half now, add more on Monday
Short it into the Monday open
questions.answer: Wait; Monday may bring a flush
questions.why: Wait. Do not buy the Friday before a possible Monday flush. Bracco finds notable capitulations and turns on Mondays. Three of the four failures we studied (BAC, WDC, KRE) were Friday buys, all stopped the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Friday's turn is often Monday's gap. Let the weekend decide.

wrong.Buy the close; the turn is in: A green Friday close does not prove the turn. A Monday gap can run through the stop.
wrong.Buy half now, add more on Monday: Half of a Friday buy still faces the gap. Our rule is one price, one stop, no adding.
wrong.Short it into the Monday open: That bets on more fall. A stretched index is Bracco's cue to watch for a turn.

questions.simple: Wait, because the real turn often comes on a Monday. Three of our four failed examples were Friday buys.

deeper.example: KRE was bought on the Friday of the tariff crash at 49.26, stop 47.09. Monday gapped to 47.50, traded 47.06 and then printed the real climax. The Friday buy was a day early, and the stop paid for it.

reasons: +1 fixed before

questions.q: On one name you may never try a parabolic long more than 3 times in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. At most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on the same stock. Each new try needs a new trigger and is a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week, six a month, each on a fresh trigger.
questions.simple: True. On one stock we try at most 3 times a week and 6 times a month, each on a new trigger.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E56)

questions.q: The peak four sessions ago was 88.00 and today's low is 50.00. How far has it fallen, in percent?
questions.why: 43.2%. The peak minus the low, over the peak: (88.00 - 50.00) / 88.00 = 43.2%. Kullamagi's premise for the long is a parabolic short that fell 50-60% or more in a few days. That is his bar. Our own DB example fell only 19.7% in 9 sessions, with four boxes ticked.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the fall from the peak to the climax low. Percent, then structure.
questions.simple: Peak minus low, divided by the peak, gives 43.2 percent.

reasons: computed key
the fall cut-offs are a held decision (D-118)

wrong.76.0%: Divided by the low instead of the peak.
wrong.38.0%: Gave the drop in dollars as a percent.
wrong.56.8%: Gave the low as a share of the peak.

questions.q: Entry 20.50, stop 19.80, the 9 EMA at 21.70. How many R to the 9 EMA?
questions.why: 1.7R. The 9 EMA minus the entry, over the entry minus the stop: (21.70 - 20.50) / (20.50 - 19.80) = 1.7R. Our card wants the 9 EMA at least 2R above the entry. At 1.7R there is no room to the target, so we pass.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the room to the 9 EMA before you buy. Under 2R, pass.
questions.simple: The room to the 9 EMA is 1.7R, under the 2R the card needs, so there is not enough room.

reasons: computed key
the 2R room is the card's proposal

wrong.2.7R: Measured the room from the stop, not the entry.
wrong.1.2R: Used the dollar room as R, no divide.
wrong.0.6R: Flipped it: divided the risk by the room.

questions.q: Where is the stop now?
questions.story: You bought at 30.00 with the stop at 29.00. Next morning it opens 28.70, under the stop. The first 30-minute bar's low is 28.50.
choices: 28.50, the first 30-minute low
Sell at the open, 28.70
No stop until it reclaims 29.00
Out; the gap is past 2R
questions.answer: 28.50, the first 30-minute low
questions.why: 28.50. A gap through the stop is the one exception to 'the stop only moves up': the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide, and the low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop. The ceiling is 2R: if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. Here the loss stays inside it.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Sell at the open, 28.70: The gap rule gives the stock 30 minutes. The open is not the decision.
wrong.No stop until it reclaims 29.00: A position always has a stop. The new one is the first 30-minute low.
wrong.Out; the gap is past 2R: The ceiling applies only if the loss goes past 2R. At the 30-minute low it does not.

questions.simple: After a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low becomes the new stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)

questions.q: Add here?
questions.story: Your parabolic long is down 1.5% from the fill, still above the stop. A friend says buy more here; the average improves.
choices: No; we do not add to a loser
Yes; the lower average is a plus
Yes, a small add is fine here
No; but widen the stop for room
questions.answer: No; we do not add to a loser
questions.why: No. Our rule is the full size at one price with one stop, so a long that is down is never added to. Bracco's own line is 'I never add when I am down'. The stop is the plan for a loser, and a better average does not make the thesis right.
questions.lesson_line: A lower average on a loser is a bigger loser. Never add down.

wrong.Yes; the lower average is a plus: A better average on a losing thesis is more risk, not a better trade.
wrong.Yes, a small add is fine here: Small is still adding. The rule is one price.
wrong.No; but widen the stop for room: Not adding is right, but the stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.simple: No. A lower average on a loser only adds risk, so we keep the one entry and the stop.

deeper.trap: The friend's pitch sounds like math: the average improves. But the stop, not the average, decides what you lose. More shares with the same stop means more dollars lost if the stop hits. A re-entry needs a new trigger, not a lower price.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)
rebalanced choices: the lone No against three Yes was a tell

questions.q: The climax day's low sits 7.3% under your fill. What does our card say?
choices: Keep the stop and cut the shares
Skip; the stop is wider than 3%
Full size; the stop is the stop
Move the stop in to fit full size
questions.answer: Keep the stop and cut the shares
questions.why: Size down by the formula. A stop between 3% and 8% away stays where it is and the shares shrink; over about 8% away, skip the trade. The usual stop within about 3% is a habit, not a wall. AGQ's stop was 7.3% away and the trade still reached 6.67R at best.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last. A wide honest stop means fewer shares.

wrong.Full size; the stop is the stop: The size comes from the stop, so a wider stop means fewer shares.
wrong.Skip; the stop is wider than 3%: Three percent is where the stop usually sits, not a wall. The card's skip line is about 8%.
wrong.Move the stop in to fit full size: A stop pulled in to fit the size is no longer the honest stop. Keep it and cut the shares.

questions.simple: The honest stop stays where it is and you buy fewer shares, because 7.3% is between 3% and 8%.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A13)
the 8% skip line is the card's proposal, a number that can change

questions.q: Our card moves the parabolic long's stop to breakeven at 2R, the low end of the house window.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The card moves the stop to breakeven at 2R, the low end of the house window. Our rule is to move it at 2R to 5R, ideally, so 2R is the early end of that range, not a separate rule.
questions.lesson_line: Two R and the stop goes to the fill. The bounce does not wait for you.
questions.simple: True. Our card moves the stop to breakeven at 2R, the earliest point of our 2R to 5R window.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, a window)
2R is the card's pick inside that window
fixed before: flagged by the cold check

questions.q: Buy now?
questions.story: The climax day gaps down 6% and keeps sliding at 10:00. It is 45% off its peak with every box ticked. Every tick looks cheaper.
choices: No; never buy before the turn
No; the gap must fill first
Yes; the gap is the buy signal
Yes, a starter now, more at VWAP
questions.answer: No; never buy before the turn
questions.why: No. Never before the turn. The buy is the first 5-minute close back over VWAP after the low. Every box ticked makes it a candidate, not a trade. Buying the gap or the low first is buying the knife, and Kullamagi says the same: do not be too early.
questions.lesson_line: Cheap is not a trigger. The reclaim is.

wrong.Yes; the gap is the buy signal: The gap is box five. The signal is the VWAP reclaim after the low.
wrong.Yes, a starter now, more at VWAP: A starter before the turn is a knife with a smaller handle. One entry, at the reclaim.
wrong.No; the gap must fill first: A gap fill is not the trigger. The buy is the first 5-minute close back over VWAP after the low.

questions.simple: No, because you wait for the turn. The buy is the first 5-minute close back over VWAP, not the gap or a cheap price.

deeper.trap: Cheap feels safe, so every tick lower looks like a better price. It is not. Until a 5-minute bar closes back over VWAP, the low may not be in. A trade under the climax low is the stop, and a new low means the selling was not done.

reasons: +2 pl.trigger_vwap is keyed while D-003 is still pending

questions.q: Bracco's post, mirrored: on the climax day, how do the opening minutes compare with the other burst days?
choices: The heaviest opening of the run
The lightest; sellers tired
About the same as other days
Heavy only if the gap filled
questions.answer: The heaviest opening of the run
questions.why: The heaviest of the run. Bracco says the climax day almost invariably shows the highest opening volume of the entire run. That is his claim for the short, and the long reads it mirrored. The card lists the opening 5 or 15 minutes as the heaviest of the run.
questions.lesson_line: The climax opens with the loudest crowd of the whole move.

wrong.The lightest; sellers tired: The climax is the panic, so the opening is the loudest, not the quietest.
wrong.About the same as other days: A climax that looks like any other day is not a climax.
wrong.Heavy only if the gap filled: Bracco ties the heavy opening to the climax day itself. Nothing in his claim depends on the gap filling.

questions.simple: Bracco says the climax day almost always has the heaviest opening volume of the run. We read it the same way for longs.

reasons: +3 the claim rests on Bracco's word for the short; no test of it on the long side

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: After the entry, a trade under the ___ low means the selling was not done.
questions.answer: climax
questions.why: The climax low. A trade under the climax low is the stop, and a new low means the selling was not done. Your stop sits a few cents under that low. The Wyckoff school reads a lower test the same way: new lows or a long consolidation.
questions.lesson_line: A new low under the climax says the panic is not finished. The stop agrees.
questions.simple: If price trades under the climax low, the panic is not over. That break is your stop.

reasons: settled stop rule A4 and F62; Wyckoff agrees

questions.q: Was the stop the mistake?
questions.story: Every box ticked. You bought at 28.50, stop 27.67. Monday's low of 27.44 took it. On March 23 the stock traded 17.95.
choices: No; a planned loss, as designed
Yes; the stop needed more room
Yes; the wrong boxes were ticked
No; sell at the close instead
questions.answer: No; a planned loss, as designed
questions.why: No. The stop is the exit, and it kept the cost of an early call to one R. The buy came in the first week of a crash from an all-time high, and a stop is what makes that survivable.
questions.lesson_line: The stop keeps a week-early call at one R. That is what it is for.

wrong.Yes; the stop needed more room: The stop only moves up, never wider. This stock traded 37% under the buy within weeks.
wrong.Yes; the wrong boxes were ticked: Every box was ticked. The problem was where in the crash the day sat.
wrong.No; sell at the close instead: The stop is a real order with the broker. Waiting for a close lets the gap set the loss.

questions.simple: No, because the stop did its job and capped the loss at one R. The crash kept going after the buy.

deeper.trap: Do not judge the stop by what came after. The stock traded 17.95 on March 23, but nobody could see that on the day you bought. The stop turns an unknowable early call into a known one-R loss.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's stop rule (A4, D41)

questions.q: Same climax, two names: both tick all five boxes. For one the index is capitulating too; for the other it is calm. Grade?
choices: The first; the market backs it
Equal; the five boxes decide
The second; a calm index is safer
The first; skip the second one
questions.answer: The first; the market backs it
questions.why: The first. The same five boxes grade higher when the index is capitulating too. A calm index, or one only starting to break down, weakens the case. Same boxes, different grade.
questions.lesson_line: Grade the market with the stock. A calm index drops the grade.

wrong.The second; a calm index is safer: A calm index means no market panic to snap back from. That weakens the case.
wrong.Equal; the five boxes decide: The boxes are the pattern. The market is the context, and context changes the grade.
wrong.The first; skip the second one: A calm index lowers the grade. Nothing in the card says it voids the trade.

questions.simple: The name with a panicking index grades higher. The market adds to the pattern, so the same boxes do not always grade the same.

reasons: +2 touches D-023 (market reading) through the new fourth choice
+1 fixed before

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: Your parabolic long reached the 9 EMA on day two and the trade is done. Two weeks later the stock has built a tight range.
choices: A new setup, a new trade, its own stop
The same trade; keep the old stop
Skip it; the snap back is already spent
Buy the range break with a wider stop
questions.answer: A new setup, a new trade, its own stop
questions.why: A new setup is a new trade with its own stop. The parabolic trade is done at the 9 EMA. A tight range can start a new trade, with its own stop and plan. Bracco sees either a fast bounce or a tight range for weeks.
questions.lesson_line: The bounce is one trade. The range after it is another, with its own stop.

wrong.The same trade; keep the old stop: The parabolic trade ended at the 9 EMA. Anything after is a new trade with its own stop and plan.
wrong.Skip it; the snap back is already spent: The first trade is spent, but a tight range can start a new trade.
wrong.Buy the range break with a wider stop: A wider stop is not the fix. The stop comes first, and if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

questions.simple: The 9 EMA ended that trade. A tight range can be a new setup, so a buy there is a new trade.

reasons: +1 rests on the card's hold-longer line (c21); the exit fraction (D-013) is held but the key no longer leans on it

questions.q: If the stock opens above a level where you planned to sell, take that sell at the open.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. If a stock opens above a level where you planned to sell, take that sell at the open. Do not wait for the close to decide. This is about planned sell levels. A gap through the stop follows the gap rule instead.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through your planned sell level is the sell. Take it at the open.
questions.simple: True. When a stock opens past a level where we planned to sell, we sell at the open.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)

questions.q: Take it?
questions.story: A $7 stock is down 55% in three days with all five boxes and a VWAP reclaim. It trades about $6 million a day.
choices: No; under $10 and $20 million a day
No; the burst is too fast to trust
Yes, half size to respect the spread
Yes; small caps are where it is common
questions.answer: No; under $10 and $20 million a day
questions.why: No. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one is $7 and about $6 million. Five boxes and a reclaim do not fix that. Bracco says the setup is more common in small caps but prefers mid to large caps.
questions.lesson_line: A textbook burst in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.Yes, half size to respect the spread: Size does not make a thin stock liquid. The rule is about the stock, not the size.
wrong.Yes; small caps are where it is common: Common is not the same as tradable. Bracco prefers mid to large caps.
wrong.No; the burst is too fast to trust: Speed is not the issue. The five boxes and the reclaim fit the pattern. The stock fails on price and volume.

questions.simple: No. The stock trades under $10 and under $20 million a day, so it fails our basic rule.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's B23 rule; D-018 is held but both options keep this key

questions.q: Which vehicles does our card prefer for this setup?
choices: Mid and large caps, plus ETFs
Small caps, where it is most common
Any cheap stock that gapped down
Only the broad index ETF itself
questions.answer: Mid and large caps, plus ETFs
questions.why: Mid and large caps, plus broad or sector ETFs. The card prefers them over small caps. Bracco says the setup is more common in small caps, but he prefers mid to large caps. Every name still needs a $10 price and $20 million a day.
questions.lesson_line: Pick the name too: mid and large caps and ETFs come first.

wrong.Only the broad index ETF itself: The card names mid and large caps and sector ETFs too, not just the index ETF.
wrong.Small caps, where it is most common: Bracco says it is more common in small caps, but he prefers mid to large caps, and so does our card.
wrong.Any cheap stock that gapped down: Price and dollars traded matter: $10 or more and $20 million a day.

questions.simple: We prefer mid and large caps and broad or sector ETFs over small caps.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, D42, E54)

questions.q: What is the read?
questions.story: On one day six names from the same hot theme print the same climax: gap downs, heavy volume, all five boxes. Each reclaims VWAP before noon.
choices: The best setting; a group unwind
Pass; many names at once means a crash
Neutral; a group changes nothing
Wait a week for a retest to form
questions.answer: The best setting; a group unwind
questions.why: The best setting. A crowded group unwinding all at once is a top setting for this setup, like the index capitulating too. HTHT was one of six names that fired that day and reached 3R the next session. Check the whole market too, since the first days of a crash are the worst setting.
questions.lesson_line: When a whole crowd gets out at once, the turn is a group event.

wrong.Wait a week for a retest to form: The buy is the VWAP reclaim on the climax day. A retest a week later is a different, later trade.
wrong.Pass; many names at once means a crash: One theme unwinding is the best setting. The start of a crash is the worst, and the state of the whole market shows it.
wrong.Neutral; a group changes nothing: A crowded group unwinding all at once is named as the best setting. It is not neutral.

questions.simple: Six names breaking down at once is a crowd leaving together. That is the best setting for this setup.

deeper.example: HTHT, July 2021, the China liquidation: six names fired on 2021-07-27. It was 29.0% off the high in 16 sessions, with a 4.5% gap down on 7.2x volume. Buy 40.75, stop 38.97, and 3R came the next session.

reasons: +1 fixed before

questions.q: A parabolic long up 2R may be held through tomorrow's earnings report.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. We hold through an earnings report only if the trade is up 5R. At 2R the trade is short of that, so it does not stay open through the report. A gap can go past the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap you cannot stop. Five R buys the ticket; 2R does not.
questions.simple: False. Hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R, and 2R is not enough.

deeper.example: GE's parabolic long reached 3R the session after its report gapped it up, so that hold carried earnings risk. A gap up pays. A gap down goes through the stop, and the gap rule then decides your exit.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's B22 rule

questions.q: Account 40,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 76.76, stop 73.20. How many shares?
questions.answer: 56 shares
questions.why: 56 shares. Risk in dollars is 40,000 x 0.5%. Divide by the fill minus the stop: 40,000 x 0.5% / (76.76 - 73.20), rounded down to 56. A 4.6% stop means fewer shares, not a tighter stop. A position cap can only make the size smaller.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Never the other way round.
questions.simple: Risk dollars divided by the gap between the fill and the stop gives 56 shares, rounded down.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A5)

choices: 57 shares
521 shares
561 shares
56 shares

wrong.57 shares: Rounded up, so the risk goes over 0.5%.
wrong.521 shares: Divided the whole account by the fill price.
wrong.561 shares: Moved the decimal on the risk percent.

questions.q: Is it a parabolic long candidate?
questions.story: Over three weeks a stock drifts from 60 to 48 in small, overlapping bars: a down day or two, then a bounce. Volume stays flat. Today it closes at the low.
choices: No; it is an orderly decline
Yes; it is already 20% down
Yes, if tomorrow gaps down hard
No; it is not an RS leader
questions.answer: No; it is an orderly decline
questions.why: No. An orderly, overlapping decline is not this setup. The fall has to accelerate with little bar overlap. A slow 20% slide is a grind, and judging by percent alone is a mistake Bracco names.
questions.lesson_line: Twenty percent down slowly is a grind. The setup needs a burst.

wrong.Yes; it is already 20% down: Percent alone is the mistake Bracco names. The structure here is a slow, overlapping drift.
wrong.Yes, if tomorrow gaps down hard: One gap into a slow grind does not make a burst. The run of steeper down days and the rising volume are still missing.
wrong.No; it is not an RS leader: Parabolic trades are exempt from the RS leader rule. The shape is what fails here.

questions.simple: No, because the fall is slow and the bars overlap. A burst gets steeper each day, and this one does not.

reasons: +1 fixed before

questions.q: What is the lesson?
questions.story: You bought a Friday turn at 25.58, stop 24.94. Monday closed 24.49, through the stop. The low came Thursday at 23.85, and by Friday the stock sat at the 9 EMA.
choices: Take the stop; selling was not done
Hold on; it reached the 9 EMA
Widen it to the Monday low
Add Monday to lower your cost
questions.answer: Take the stop; selling was not done
questions.why: Take the stop. A trade under the climax low is the stop, and a new low means the selling was not done. Here Monday closed through the 24.94 stop, the low came days later at 23.85, and the stock reached the 9 EMA only by Friday. The later turn, not the Friday turn, was the trade.
questions.lesson_line: The first turn is often a day early. The stop costs one R; the next turn is a new trade.

wrong.Hold on; it reached the 9 EMA: It got there from a lower low. Holding through the stop is how one R becomes more.
wrong.Widen it to the Monday low: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Add Monday to lower your cost: Never add when down. A re-entry needs a new trigger, as a new trade.

questions.simple: Take the stop. Price closed through it, and a new low means the selling is not done.

deeper.trap: The hard part is that the first turn looked right: a gap-down day, bought on the reclaim, on a Friday. Three of the four failed examples on our bars were Friday buys, with the real low printing on the Monday or later. The card says not to buy the Friday before a possible Monday flush.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)
worked example from our own bars, not yet reviewed by the owner
fixed before: the key was the only choice phrased as an observation

questions.q: 3x ETFs are the preferred vehicles for the index version, with no extra rules.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our rulebook prefers 3x ETFs, with no extra rules, and the card names them the preferred vehicles for the index version of this setup. No extra rules means the same trigger, stop and size rules apply as for a stock.
questions.lesson_line: For the index turn, the 3x ETF is the tool, not the exception.
questions.simple: True. We prefer 3x ETFs for the index version of this setup, and they get no special rules.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E54)

questions.q: The stock trades 500,000 shares a day on average. Our ceiling on the position?
choices: 5,000 shares
10,000 shares
2,500 shares
50,000 shares
questions.answer: 5,000 shares
questions.why: 5,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 500,000 is 5,000. Illiquid names are not even watched. This is a separate ceiling from the risk-based size and the position cap.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume. In a panic, getting out is the whole game.

wrong.10,000 shares: That is double our ceiling. The limit is 1% of the average daily volume, which is 5,000 shares.
wrong.2,500 shares: That is half the ceiling, not the ceiling. One percent of 500,000 is 5,000.
wrong.50,000 shares: That is a tenth of the daily volume, ten times our 1% limit.

questions.simple: The ceiling is 1% of the daily volume, so 1% of 500,000 shares is 5,000 shares.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)
its 3x ETF liquidity exception is a held decision (D-018)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought at 52.00 with the stop at 50.90. Next morning it opens 49.50. The first 30-minute bar's low is 48.70.
choices: Out; a 3R loss is past the 2R cap
48.70 is the new stop; hold on
Hold and wait for the close
Sell half now, hold half
questions.answer: Out; a 3R loss is past the 2R cap
questions.why: Out. After a gap through the stop, the first 30 minutes decide. The first 30-minute low becomes the new stop, with a ceiling: if the loss goes past 2R, get out. Your risk was the distance from 52.00 down to the 50.90 stop. A loss to 48.70 is a 3R loss.
questions.lesson_line: The gap rule has a ceiling. Past 2R in the first 30 minutes, you are done.

wrong.48.70 is the new stop; hold on: The 30-minute low becomes the stop only when the loss stays inside 2R. Here it is three times the risk.
wrong.Hold and wait for the close: The first 30 minutes decide, not the close.
wrong.Sell half now, hold half: The rule gives two outcomes: a new stop at the 30-minute low, or out past 2R. Half is neither.

questions.simple: Get out. The first 30 minutes took the loss past 2R, so the rule says to leave.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's gap rule (B20)
+2 the key needs arithmetic: 48.70 is a 3R loss

questions.q: For the blow-off unwind, what came before the fall?
choices: A 50%+ run in days or weeks
A quiet base near highs
A slow downtrend of months
An earnings gap, then a fade
questions.answer: A 50%+ run in days or weeks
questions.why: A parabolic run of 50% or more in days or weeks. For the blow-off unwind, the stock was a parabolic-short candidate in the prior 20 sessions. Kullamagi's premise is a successful parabolic short that then falls 50-60% or more in a few days.
questions.lesson_line: The unwind needs a blow-off before it. No run, no rubber band.

wrong.A quiet base near highs: A quiet base is not a run. The unwind follows a stock that was a parabolic-short candidate.
wrong.A slow downtrend of months: That is the other context, a capitulation in a decline. The blow-off unwind starts from a run up.
wrong.An earnings gap, then a fade: One gap and a fade is not a run of 50% or more in days or weeks.

questions.simple: Before an unwind comes a blow-off. The stock ran up 50% or more in days or weeks first.

reasons: +3 the 50% run rests on one card line (c29)
+2 a proposed threshold that can change

questions.q: Which setup is it?
questions.story: A stock has three straight up days and two gap-up opens, each day a bigger gain than the last. Today it gaps up again, then breaks under VWAP by 10:30.
choices: A parabolic short; the burst ran up
A parabolic long; the gap is the climax
A U&R long; it undercut intraday VWAP
Neither; a burst needs five full days
questions.answer: A parabolic short; the burst ran up
questions.why: A parabolic short. The burst runs up and the climax gaps up. The short is taken as it breaks under VWAP, with the stop over the day's high. The long is the same five boxes mirrored: a burst down and a gap down.
questions.lesson_line: Which way did it gap. Up is the short, down is the long.

wrong.A parabolic long; the gap is the climax: The long's climax gaps down. This one gapped up after three up days.
wrong.A U&R long; it undercut intraday VWAP: A U&R undercuts a visible low after a dip, not VWAP. Three vertical up days into a gap is a burst.
wrong.Neither; a burst needs five full days: The burst is 3 to 5 days and the climax gap usually comes on day 3 to 5. These days already fit.

questions.simple: It is a parabolic short because the stock ran up and gapped up. The long is the same pattern upside down.

deeper.trap: The long and the short share the same five boxes, so only the direction tells them apart. Check which way the climax gap points before you pick a side. Up is the short, entered as it breaks under VWAP with the stop over the high. Down is the long, entered on a reclaim over VWAP with the stop under the low.

reasons: +2 pl.climax_gap is held (D-119); the gap is taught as a tell, not a gate

questions.q: Which card?
questions.story: A leader fresh out of a base drops 2 ATR in one afternoon into its old high. No low is undercut. The volume is the day's heaviest, then it turns. Yesterday it closed at a high.
choices: Mean Reversion form A; a one-day flush
A parabolic long; it fell 2 ATR
A U&R; the old high is the level
A dead-cat bounce; a one-day fall
questions.answer: Mean Reversion form A; a one-day flush
questions.why: Mean Reversion form A. Bracco's one-day flush in a leader into a level is that card. A parabolic long needs 3 to 5 straight down days with two gap downs. Count the down days first.
questions.lesson_line: Count the down days. One day in a leader is Mean Reversion; three to five is parabolic.

wrong.A parabolic long; it fell 2 ATR: One afternoon is not a burst. The burst is 3 to 5 straight down days with two gap downs.
wrong.A U&R; the old high is the level: A U&R needs an undercut of a visible low after a small dip. Here no low is undercut; it is a 2 ATR flush into a level.
wrong.A dead-cat bounce; a one-day fall: A dead-cat bounce starts with a one-day gap down of 15% to 70%. This is a 2 ATR afternoon flush in a leader.

questions.simple: It is a one-day flush in a leader, so it is Mean Reversion. A parabolic long needs 3 to 5 down days in a row.

deeper.trap: Count the days before you name the card. One heavy afternoon in a leader fits Mean Reversion, even with big volume and a quick turn. A parabolic long needs the whole burst behind it: 3 to 5 straight down days, two gap downs and rising volume. Heavy volume alone names neither card.

reasons: card lookalike row; Mean Reversion is taught in another unit

questions.q: Which family?
questions.story: A 2x-3x ETF is 20% under its 200-day after a four-day, 60% fall with two gap downs. The index is capitulating too. After the low, the ETF reclaims VWAP.
choices: Parabolic; a U&R needs a level
A U&R; VWAP is the level
A flat base; wait for the pivot
Not tradable; it is under the 200-day
questions.answer: Parabolic; a U&R needs a level
questions.why: The parabolic family. A U&R undercuts a visible low after a dip of a few percent, in a name above its 200-day. A parabolic long needs no level. Below the 200-day, a stock is a hard no, but a 2x-3x ETF may be bought there on a parabolic long. This one fits.
questions.lesson_line: No level, under the 200-day, a 2x-3x ETF after a crash: that is parabolic territory, not a U&R.

wrong.A U&R; VWAP is the level: VWAP is the trigger, not a level. A U&R needs a visible low and a name above its 200-day.
wrong.A flat base; wait for the pivot: Nothing is basing. A four-day crash is a burst.
wrong.Not tradable; it is under the 200-day: Below the 200-day, a stock is a hard no. A 2x-3x ETF may be bought there on a parabolic long, and this one is.

questions.simple: Parabolic, because a U&R needs a visible level and this ETF has none. A 2x-3x ETF may sit under the 200-day.

deeper.trap: Below the 200-day, stocks are a hard no. The exception is an index or a 2x-3x ETF on a parabolic long. Do not stretch it to a U&R. A U&R needs a visible low and a name above its 200-day. A parabolic long needs no level and may sit under it.

reasons: +2 D-009 (the 200-day exception) is held; only B26's own exception is keyed

questions.q: Hidden ticker; the chart ends on a gap-down day. How many of the five boxes does it show?
choices: Five of five
Four of five
Three of five
Two of five
questions.answer: Five of five
questions.why: All five. The card counts this chart 5 of 5: a 25.6% fall in 8 sessions, a 2.2% gap down on 3.5x volume, and a close 2.8% off the open. The boxes read the fall; the market reading has to say whether the selling is done.
questions.lesson_line: Five boxes and a strong close on the gap-down day. That is the picture.

wrong.Four of five: The card counts all five boxes on this chart, so none is missing.
wrong.Three of five: The card counts all five boxes on this chart, so none is missing.
wrong.Two of five: The card counts all five boxes on this chart, so none is missing.

questions.simple: All five boxes show. The boxes read the fall, and the market has to say whether the selling is done.

deeper.trap: Five boxes are not a guarantee. At the start of one crash, 83 names printed a gap-down reversal day on heavy volume with every box ticked, and none reached 5R. It was the first week of a breakdown, so the boxes read the fall and the market has to say whether the selling is done.

reasons: a worked example read from our own bars
the box count is a held decision (D-002)
fixed before: the old key had no balanced second 'Take it' choice

questions.q: Hidden ticker; the chart ends on a gap-down day whose volume ran 1.5 times its average. Take it or pass.
choices: Pass; its own volume falls short
Take it; the boxes are ticked
Take it; the gap is enough
Pass; the whole market is falling
questions.answer: Pass; its own volume falls short
questions.why: Pass. The climax day ends at 2 times its 50-day average volume or more, and this one ran 1.5 times. Four boxes were ticked, but the volume climax was in the index (SPY 4.1x), not in this name.
questions.lesson_line: The crowd has to be in this stock, not just in the index.

wrong.Take it; the boxes are ticked: Four of five boxes were there. Volume is its own gate and it missed.
wrong.Take it; the gap is enough: The gap is box five. The climax volume is a separate rule.
wrong.Pass; the whole market is falling: A falling market is not a reason to pass. An index capitulating too is the best setting. The fault here is this stock's own volume.

questions.simple: Pass, because the volume was only 1.5 times average and the rule needs 2 times. The crowd was in the index, not this stock.

deeper.example: APD on the tariff-crash Monday, 2025-04-07. It had four of five boxes and a 1.7% gap. Its volume was 1.5x its average, while SPY ran 4.1x. The rule needs 2x. Taken anyway, it was stopped the next day at 243.69.

reasons: +2 the 2x line is a card proposal and can change

questions.q: Bracco says notable capitulations and turns have occurred on a Monday.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Bracco's Monday Effect: through his studies, notable capitulations and turns have occurred on a Monday. DB was a Monday climax in our examples. It is his observation, not a guarantee.
questions.lesson_line: Bracco's best turns have come on Mondays. Do not buy the Friday before one.
questions.simple: True. Bracco says his studies found notable capitulations and turns on a Monday.

deeper.trap: Do not turn this into a rule that every Monday is a buy. It is Bracco's observation that notable turns have come on Mondays. It is also why we do not buy the Friday before one: three of our four failures were Friday buys.

reasons: +3 the Monday effect rests on Bracco's own studies, one cited source

questions.q: Fill 20.50. The climax low is 19.00 and the stop sits five cents under it. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 7.56%. The stop is five cents under the 19.00 low. The fill minus the stop, over the fill: (20.50 - (19.00 - 0.05)) / 20.50 = 7.56%. That is between 3% and 8%, so we keep the honest stop and size down by the formula. Over about 8% we would skip. SLG's stop was 7.2% away and it reached 3R in 6 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the honest stop before the size. Wide but under 8% is fewer shares, not no trade.
questions.simple: The stop is 7.56% below the fill, between 3% and 8%, so you buy fewer shares instead of skipping.

deeper.trap: Do not tighten the stop to make the percent look smaller. The stop sits a few cents under the climax low because a new low means the selling was not done. A tighter stop only hides the true distance, and the formula then sizes you too big for the risk.

reasons: computed key
the 8% skip line is the card's proposal, a number that can change

wrong.8.18%: Divided by the stop instead of the fill.
wrong.9.76%: Read five cents as fifty cents under the low.
wrong.92.44%: Gave the stop as a share of the fill.

questions.q: What does the rulebook say?
questions.story: Ten trading days after the climax your parabolic long sits at 0.6R. The stop was never touched and the 9 EMA is still above.
choices: Sold; under 1R after 10 sessions
Hold; the stop was never hit
Add; it proved the low is in
Raise the stop; wait a month
questions.answer: Sold; under 1R after 10 sessions
questions.why: Sold. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, which frees the money. That holds even though the stop was never touched. Bracco says these are short-lived trades, not held longer than 1-3 days.
questions.lesson_line: This bounce lives for days. Ten days under 1R and the money has a better home.

wrong.Hold; the stop was never hit: The stop is one exit. Time is the other. Bracco holds these trades 1 to 3 days.
wrong.Add; it proved the low is in: Our rule is full size at one price with one stop, no adding. A bounce that went nowhere is not proof.
wrong.Raise the stop; wait a month: The rule sells a trade under 1R after 10 trading days. A month is far past that.

questions.simple: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, and a snap back should not need that long.

deeper.trap: The stop is not the only exit. Time is another. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is tying up money that a fresh setup could use.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's C33 rule; D-019 may shorten the time stop, and this key holds under both options

questions.q: In our test, most longs reached the 9 EMA before the day's low broke, as Bracco's magnet claim says for the short.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The mirror is not true for longs. In our test only about 4 in 10 reached the 9 EMA before the day's low broke. The 9 EMA is still the target, but it is not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: The 9 EMA is the target, not a promise. Four in ten get there.
questions.simple: False. In our test only about 4 in 10 longs reached the 9 EMA before the day's low broke.

deeper.counter: Bracco's claim is from his studies of the short: the 9-day EMA acts as a magnet for mean reversion. Our own daily test of longs found only about 4 in 10 reached it before the day's low broke. After a crash from far above, the 9 EMA can be out of reach, as with CAR and AGQ.

reasons: +3 the 4 in 10 comes from one card line (c19)
+2 a number from our own test that can change

questions.q: After a three-session crash from 847.70 to 202.31, CAR's 9 EMA was still above 260 at the end of April. What does our card warn?
choices: Do not count on reaching the 9 EMA
Count on the 9 EMA in days
Expect an equal-size bounce
Widen the stop for more time
questions.answer: Do not count on reaching the 9 EMA
questions.why: Do not count on the 9 EMA every time. After CAR's three-session crash from 847.70 to 202.31, its 9 EMA, above 260 at the end of April, was not reached until 05-21. Expecting the 9 EMA every time is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Room to the target is good. A target in another zip code is a warning.

wrong.Count on the 9 EMA in days: After a crash from far above it can take weeks. CAR did not get there until 05-21.
wrong.Expect an equal-size bounce: A bigger crash puts the 9 EMA farther away. The card promises no bigger bounce.
wrong.Widen the stop for more time: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.simple: After a crash from far above, the 9 EMA can be too far away to reach for weeks.

deeper.counter: Bracco's magnet claim for the 9 EMA is for his short. The card says the mirror is not true for longs. CAR fell from 847.70 to 202.31 in three sessions, and its 9 EMA, above 260 at the end of April, was not reached until 05-21.

reasons: a worked example read from our own bars
a date that changes with the data
the quote sits in the criteria card, not the research note the source cites

questions.q: What decides?
questions.story: On one Friday 83 names print the climax: every box ticked, every context met, heavy volume. It is the first week of a slide from an all-time high.
choices: The market reading, not the bars
The box count; five beats four
The volume; the heaviest day wins
The RS rating; leaders hold up best
questions.answer: The market reading, not the bars
questions.why: The market reading, not the bars. All 83 names had every box ticked, every context met and heavy volume, yet none reached 5R and all were stopped. It was the first week of a breakdown from an all-time high, and the real low came 16 sessions later. That is a market starting down, not one crowded group unwinding. The rule reads the climax. The market reading has to say whether the selling is done.
questions.lesson_line: Perfect bars in the first week of a crash are still the first week of a crash.

wrong.The box count; five beats four: Every one of the 83 had every box. The count could not separate them.
wrong.The volume; the heaviest day wins: Volume was heavy across the board. It could not tell the failures from a real turn.
wrong.The RS rating; leaders hold up best: Parabolic trades have no RS requirement, and all 83 were stopped, leaders or not.

questions.simple: The market reading decides, since the bars cannot show it. Perfect bars in the first week of a crash failed all 83 times.

deeper.example: On 2020-02-28, 83 names printed a gap-down reversal on heavy volume with every box and context ticked. None reached 5R and all were stopped. BAC was one: bought 28.50, stopped at 27.67, and it traded 17.95 on 03-23.

reasons: +2 the 83 and 16 come from one dated read of our own data

questions.q: What is the lesson?
questions.story: A regional bank has fallen hard in a panic, and the setup fits. You buy at 23.10 with the stop at 21.70. Day one closes at 21.27, down 7.9%, and you are stopped out. Six sessions later, in the same panic, a different name turned and ran.
choices: The buy came one leg too early
Never buy a bank in a panic
Widen the stop on the next buy
The setup was false from the start
questions.answer: The buy came one leg too early
questions.why: The buy came one leg too early. This panic had one more leg. The stop kept the cost to one R, and the later turn was a new trade.
questions.lesson_line: A turn in a panic can come one leg early. Let the stop pay for it.

wrong.Never buy a bank in a panic: The sector was not the problem. The timing inside the panic was.
wrong.Widen the stop on the next buy: A wider stop would have paid more for the same wrong day. The stop only moves up.
wrong.The setup was false from the start: The setup fit. The panic simply had one more leg, and the stop did its job.

questions.simple: The buy was a leg too early, and the stop kept the loss small. The panic had one more leg to run.

deeper.trap: Being early is the price of reading a climax from the bars. BKU fit the setup and was stopped on day one: it closed down 7.9%, and the panic ran to 19.04. SLG turned six sessions later. The stop under the climax low keeps the cost of being early to one R.

reasons: +1 fixed before

questions.q: Buy again?
questions.story: You were stopped out of a parabolic long on Tuesday. Thursday the same stock prints a new low, turns, and reclaims VWAP again, with every box and rule still met. It would be your second try this week.
choices: Yes; a new trade with its own stop
No; a stop-out ends that setup
Yes, but with a wider stop this time
No; wait until it reaches the 9 EMA
questions.answer: Yes; a new trade with its own stop
questions.why: Yes, as a new trade. After a stop-out we buy again only if the setup triggers again, with its own stop and every rule. The stock made a new low, turned and reclaimed VWAP, so the trigger fired again. It is the second try this week, inside the limit of 3 in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a verdict on the setup. The next reclaim is a new trade.

wrong.No; a stop-out ends that setup: After a stop-out we buy again if the setup triggers again, as a new trade. A stop-out does not end the setup.
wrong.Yes, but with a wider stop this time: A new trade gets its stop a few cents under its own low, not a wider one to dodge a repeat.
wrong.No; wait until it reaches the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA is the target, not the trigger. The trigger is the reclaim.

questions.simple: Yes. A stop-out is not a ban, so a fresh trigger is a new trade with its own stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is buying back to get even. Each try needs its own trigger, stop and size, and the count stops at 3 a week and 6 a month on one stock. A stop-out says this try failed, not that the setup is dead.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21, E56)

questions.q: The run's low was 20.00 and the peak 34.00. The run before the unwind, in percent?
questions.why: 70%. The run is the peak over the run's low, minus one: 34.00 over 20.00 is 70% more. The blow-off unwind wants a prior run of 50% or more in days or weeks, the premise of Kullamagi's successful parabolic short.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the run before the fall. The rubber band needs the stretch first.
questions.simple: The peak is 70% above the run's low. That is past the 50% run the unwind needs.

deeper.trap: The percent depends on the base. From the low, 20.00 to 34.00 is 70% up. The drop back from 34.00 to 20.00 is a smaller percent, because it is measured from the higher price. Use the run's low as the base for the run.

reasons: +2 a computed key (pct_change, recomputed by the validator)

wrong.41.2%: Divided by the peak instead of the low.
wrong.14.0%: Gave the gap in dollars as a percent.
wrong.58.8%: Gave the low as a share of the peak.

questions.q: Take it?
questions.story: A 3x inverse Nasdaq ETF is 35% off its high with all five boxes ticked. The index is rallying to new highs.
choices: No; its climax is the index peak
Yes; the boxes fit the pattern
Yes; inverse funds snap harder
No; 3x funds are too risky
questions.answer: No; its climax is the index peak
questions.why: No. An inverse fund's selling climax is simply the index making a high. A bounce there is a bet on an index pullback, a different setup with different odds. SQQQ with all five boxes made 0.01R.
questions.lesson_line: An inverse fund does not capitulate. The index does, and this is its mirror image.

wrong.Yes; the boxes fit the pattern: The boxes describe a stock's panic. Here they describe the index's strength.
wrong.Yes; inverse funds snap harder: They snap back only if the index pulls back. That is a different trade with different odds.
wrong.No; 3x funds are too risky: 3x ETFs are the preferred vehicles for the index version, with no extra rules. The problem here is that it is inverse.

questions.simple: No, because an inverse fund falls when the index rises. Its bounce is only a bet on an index pullback.

deeper.trap: The chart looks perfect: a 35% fall, all five boxes, a gap down, heavy volume. But the fund's fall is the index rising. Read what the fund holds before you read its candles. SQQQ in 2020 ticked all five boxes and made 0.01R.

reasons: card no-trade row and a dated example agree

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, target.
questions.story: BABA, 2022-03-15: 43.4% off the high in 17 sessions, all five boxes, a 3.4% gap down on 3.6x volume. Say it reclaims VWAP after the low.
choices: Buy reclaim, stop under low, 9 EMA
Buy open, stop at 200-day, 9 EMA
Buy reclaim, 200-day stop, high
Buy close, stop under low, high
questions.answer: Buy reclaim, stop under low, 9 EMA
questions.why: Buy the reclaim at market, put the stop a few cents under the climax low, and target the daily 9 EMA. Entries are market orders, and the full size goes in at one price. On our bars BABA closed 2.2% above its open and reached 3R the next session. A stock this far under its 200-day is a hard no today, so this is a drill. Only an index or a 2x-3x ETF gets this plan. Know the exit before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Entry at the reclaim, stop under the low, target the 9 EMA. Write it before the turn.

wrong.Buy open, stop at 200-day, 9 EMA: The open is before the turn, and the stop sits a few cents under the climax low, not the 200-day.
wrong.Buy reclaim, 200-day stop, high: The stop sits a few cents under the climax low, not the 200-day, and the target is the daily 9 EMA, not the old high.
wrong.Buy close, stop under low, high: The buy is the intraday reclaim, not the close, and the target is the daily 9 EMA, not the old high.

questions.simple: Buy the VWAP reclaim at market, set the stop a few cents under the low, and aim for the 9 EMA.

deeper.example: BABA, 2022-03-15: our bars use the close, 76.76, as the fill, with the stop at 73.20, 4.6% away. 3R came the next session and 13R was the best. MCHI, FXI and QFIN fired the same day and all reached 5R.

reasons: the trigger is the card's default while D-003 is pending
a worked example read from our own bars
fixed before: the key tied the longest choice

questions.q: Take it?
questions.story: Monday, after a slide that is already weeks old. The index gaps down more than an ATR, four ATR under its 50-day; the VIX jumps to 31. A liquid ETF prints all five boxes on 3x volume and reclaims VWAP at 10:40.
choices: Take it; the context and trigger agree
Pass; a VIX over 30 means more downside
Pass; a Monday gap is a trap
Take it at the open, ahead of VWAP
questions.answer: Take it; the context and trigger agree
questions.why: Take it. The index is capitulating too. It gapped down more than an ATR, sits four ATR under its 50-day, and it is a Monday. The VIX moved fast into 30. The slide is weeks old, not a fresh breakdown. The ETF also reclaimed VWAP, so the trigger printed.
questions.lesson_line: A Monday gap with the VIX spiking and the index stretched: that is the day.

wrong.Pass; a VIX over 30 means more downside: A fast move into 30 is Bracco's cue to look for a turn, not to run from it.
wrong.Pass; a Monday gap is a trap: Bracco finds notable capitulations and turns on Mondays. The Monday gap is the cue, not a trap.
wrong.Take it at the open, ahead of VWAP: Never before the turn. The buy is the first 5-minute close back over VWAP, here at 10:40.

questions.simple: Take it. The whole market is panicking, it is a Monday, and the ETF has reclaimed VWAP, so the buy has printed.

deeper.trap: A big VIX scares people into passing. Bracco reads a fast move into 30 as the time to watch for a turn. Our rule then waits for the reclaim before acting. Here the reclaim printed at 10:40 on 3x volume with the index stretched. That is the setup in full.

reasons: +1 fixed before

questions.q: The Model Book's old Parabolic Long card says ride a stock up its vertical run. What is our parabolic long?
choices: The burst mirrored: crash, then turn
The same; ride the run bar by bar
A short at the top of the run
questions.answer: The burst mirrored: crash, then turn
questions.why: The mirror of Bracco's burst: a burst down, then the turn. Our rulebook makes the long the mirror image; the old card describes the opposite trade and is overruled.
questions.lesson_line: Our parabolic long buys the crash's end, not the run's middle.

wrong.The same; ride the run bar by bar: That is the overruled card. Riding the run is the parabolic short's setup, from the other side.
wrong.A short at the top of the run: That is the parabolic short. The long is its mirror, after the fall.

questions.q: Entry 40.00, stop 38.50, the 9 EMA at 45.10. Where is 3R, and is it below or above the 9 EMA?
choices: 44.50, below the 9 EMA
43.00, below 9 EMA
46.00, over the 9 EMA
47.50, above 9 EMA
questions.answer: 44.50, below the 9 EMA
questions.why: 3R is at 44.50, below the 9 EMA at 45.10. One R is the fill minus the stop, and 3R sits three of those above the fill. The card wants the 9 EMA at least 2R above the entry, and here it is more than 3R away, so there is room.
questions.lesson_line: Mark 3R and the 9 EMA on the chart. Know which one price meets first.

wrong.43.00, below 9 EMA: 43.00 is only 2R: two times the risk above the fill. 3R is three times.
wrong.46.00, over the 9 EMA: 46.00 is above 3R, four times the risk above the fill. 3R is three times.
wrong.47.50, above 9 EMA: 47.50 is well past 3R. 3R is three times the risk above the fill.

questions.simple: 3R is 44.50, a little below the 9 EMA at 45.10.

deeper.example: From the fill at 40.00 the levels run in order: 2R, then 3R at 44.50, then the 9 EMA at 45.10. Mark all three on the chart once you are filled, so you know which one price meets first.

reasons: computed key

questions.q: What happened next, and why?
questions.story: All five boxes, a close at the top of the range, 7.4% off the open. The index has just lost its 200-day for the first time in a year. A perfect-looking V.
choices: A new low next day; a fresh breakdown
3R the next session; a textbook V
Flat for a month; no edge either way
questions.answer: A new low next day; a fresh breakdown
questions.why: A new low the next day. A perfect-looking V in a fresh breakdown is the worst setting; NBIS fell 12.2% the next session. The first days of a breakdown are not this setup.
questions.lesson_line: A V on the first leg of a breakdown is a trap with a nice shape.

wrong.3R the next session; a textbook V: The shape was textbook. The place in the move was the first leg down.
wrong.Flat for a month; no edge either way: Fresh breakdowns do not go flat. They go lower.

questions.q: On Bracco's line, which burst is stronger?
questions.story: Two stocks print a climax day in the same context. One ticks all five boxes. The other misses the rising-volume box.
choices: The burst with all five boxes
The burst missing the volume box
Equal; the box count adds nothing
Neither; a burst needs all five boxes
questions.answer: The burst with all five boxes
questions.why: The all-five burst. On Bracco's line, not every box needs to be satisfied, but the more boxes checked, the stronger the setup. The five boxes are three lower closes, two gap downs, bigger losses, rising volume and a climax gap down.
questions.lesson_line: More boxes ticked reads stronger, on Bracco's line. Not every box is needed.

wrong.Equal; the box count adds nothing: Bracco's line is that the more boxes checked, the stronger the setup. The boxes matter.
wrong.The burst missing the volume box: One box fewer is a weaker read on Bracco's line, not a stronger one.
wrong.Neither; a burst needs all five boxes: On Bracco's line not every box is needed. A burst one box short is weaker, not a pass.

questions.simple: The burst with all five boxes is stronger. Bracco says not every box is needed, but more boxes make it stronger.

questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Our rulebook allows no new buys outside regular trading hours. A deep pre-market gap-down is not a buy, however much it looks like the low.
questions.lesson_line: Regular hours only. A deep pre-market gap is not a buy.

questions.q: How do we decide the first sell on a winner?
choices: A judgment; day 3 or later is usual
Always a third of the shares at 3R
Half of the shares at 2R, always
Sell it all on day 1 of the buy
questions.answer: A judgment; day 3 or later is usual
questions.why: A judgment. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later, into a push.
questions.simple: It is a judgment, usually on day 3 or later, into a push.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19: the hard rule for the first trim)

wrong.Always a third of the shares at 3R: The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
wrong.Half of the shares at 2R, always: Two R is where the stop can move to breakeven, not a fixed place to sell half.
wrong.Sell it all on day 1 of the buy: We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy, and selling all of it is not a first sell.

questions.story: A liquid ETF has closed lower three days running, and each drop was bigger than the last: 1.0%, then 1.8%, then 3.0%. Today it opens flat, drifts lower, then climbs back over VWAP at 10:45.
questions.q: A friend says the VWAP reclaim is the buy. What do you do?
choices: Pass; there is no gap-down climax day
Buy; three lower closes are enough
Buy; it just reclaimed VWAP
Buy half now and half on a gap down
questions.answer: Pass; there is no gap-down climax day
questions.why: Pass. The buy day is the climax day, the gap-down day. Here the drops grew from 1.0% to 1.8% to 3.0%, but today opened flat, so there is no climax gap. The VWAP reclaim is the trigger only on a climax day, after the low is in.
questions.lesson_line: No gap-down climax, no buy. A VWAP reclaim alone is not the trigger.
questions.simple: Pass. The buy day is the gap-down climax day, and today opened flat, so the VWAP reclaim alone is not a buy.

wrong.Buy; three lower closes are enough: Three lower closes are only the first box. The buy day itself must gap down.
wrong.Buy; it just reclaimed VWAP: The reclaim is the trigger only on a climax day, after the low is in. Today is not one.
wrong.Buy half now and half on a gap down: The setup is one entry, the full size at one price, with no second entry. Buying before the climax day is buying early.
